articles.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
articles.description: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. Together they established the Trilateral Arctic Pacific Partnership (TAPP), an initiative focused on maritime safety, emergency response and economic cooperation in the North. There are good reasons for the United States to pursue this now. Japan and South Korea are developing their commercial interests in the region and both countries are experts in polar research and maritime operations. This initiative opens up new diplomatic options for Washington in the Arctic, particularly as relations have been tense with other Arctic nations. Much of that tension, of course, has been self-inflicted, with recent threats by President Donald Trump to take over Greenland, provoking a diplomatic crisis with Denmark and the rest of the European Union. While the agreement between the U.S., Denmark and Greenland has eased tensions, it didn’t fully heal the damage done to transatlantic trust. articles.title: Trump-Xi-Putin meet could be more important than you think
articles.description: The trilateral summit scheduled between President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping should be seen as the first tentative step towards — ideally — a “concert of powers” in which the leading states of the world will manage relations between themselves in such a way as to preserve and promote international peace. In this way, even if the meeting — which is supposed to take place Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit — leads to no concrete results, it will still be worth doing. If the ultimate goal is peace and any possibility of co-operation against transnational threats including climate change, rogue AI, and terrorism, it must begin with the fostering of reasonably stable relations between the world’s three most powerful military states. articles.title: "Major Shift" In Classic-Car Market Sends '80s And '90s Autos Surging While Baby Boomer Classics Stall
articles.description: "Major Shift" In Classic-Car Market Sends '80s And '90s Autos Surging While Baby Boomer Classics Stall The Great Wealth Transfer from baby boomers to millennials and other younger generations involves much more than the junk in the attic, jewelry, and whatever else boomers collected or cherished. It sometimes includes a garage full of classic cars that younger generations seem to have little interest in, whether because tastes have changed or because they don't have the money to collect them. Auto blog Carscoops reports that 12 million collector cars worth $570 billion could pass to the next generation over the next 15 years. In total, there are more than 43 million collectible vehicles across the US. articles.title: The Limits Of Control: Why Human Nature Will Defeat China's AI Socialism
articles.description: The Limits Of Control: Why Human Nature Will Defeat China's AI Socialism Authored by Stu Cvrk via The Epoch Times , Beijing is betting that artificial intelligence (AI) can do what Gosplan never could : see everything, predict everything, and steer 1.4 billion people without the information failures that sank Soviet planning. The bet will probably make the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) better at control than any regime before it. But it will not make socialism work. The flaw in every planned society was never a shortage of data. It was human nature: people lie to those who watch them, officials protect themselves, and nobody can be ordered to care. AI does not cure those problems. It inherits them, scales them, and hides them behind a dashboard. The Machine in Brief The control apparatus already in place is vast. Some 600 million to 700 million cameras feed municipal "city brain" platforms that use face and gait recognition and flag crowds. Grid workers and volunteer informants watch neighborhoods of a few hundred households each. Blacklists bar "untrustworthy" people from planes, trains, and loans. Contrary to Western myth, though, there is still no single national personal score.

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
articles.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Like many men of his generation, he tends to push his feelings down from his heart to his toes’: Meera Sodha on her father’s homecoming
articles.description: After a childhood of grief, hardship and hunger, the Guardian food writer’s father Raj always resisted going back to Uganda. What happened when he finally agreed to accompany her on a bittersweet journey into the past? The moment I step off the plane and on to the soil of Entebbe it hits me. Uganda is in my blood. This country that had once existed only in my imagination is finally real. The heat is heavy, the earth bright and rich like dark terracotta. I want to capture this moment – me with my 75-year-old dad, back where he was born. A place he never imagined he would return to. I whoop and reach for my camera, turn it towards my father’s face. “You’re back!” I say. Continue reading...

articles.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: The 14 best men’s boots for winter, from chelseas and lace-ups to wellies
articles.description: Whether you want minimalist or heritage, waterproof or suede, our menswear expert has rounded up the most stylish pairs for every occasion and outfit • The best men’s coats for autumn and winter I haven’t always worn boots. For years I wrote them off – at 5ft 8in, I was convinced anything above the ankle would make my legs look shorter. Then I started wearing them with the right trousers – a straight leg that falls over the top – and realised I’d spent a decade getting winter wrong. All anyone sees is a smart pair of shoes that happens to keep your ankles warm. Here’s the thing: boots needn’t be intimidating. They’re just the wintry version of the leather shoes you already own. A chelsea is your loafer – it goes with pretty much everything in your wardrobe and every event in your diary, Christmas parties included. A derby boot is laced up, a bit sturdier and just as happy with jeans. The chukka is your weekend trainer. And the chunky, rubber-soled ones? Just think of them as an umbrella for your feet. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
articles.description: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘You unpack once’: despite reports of ‘poop cruises’ and murder, cruise ships are more popular than ever
articles.description: High-profile crimes and disease outbreaks obscure the fact that the big ships are largely safe – and seeing record numbers of bookings This month, there has been a swell of stories about things going wrong on cruises. A man was arrested in Texas after he allegedly killed a woman during a voyage through the Caribbean. A pianist on a Royal Caribbean cruise from California was rescued by two fishers in the Pacific Ocean after he went overboard. And Singapore seized the MV Odyssey, a US-operated cruise ship that was supposed to offer retirees a “permanent” life at sea. The operator ran out of money because of increased fuel prices and dropped all its passengers off in Cambodia. Continue reading...

articles.title: Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko are your new culture guides: best podcasts of the week
articles.description: The Guardian’s new twice-weekly show unpicks all the biggest cultural moments. Plus, what is it like to grow up as a YouTube kidfluencer? Is SNL UK funnier than the original? Does it matter if a pop star can sing? The Guardian’s Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko host this twice-weekly culture videocast . On Thursdays, they zoom in on a big cultural moment with fresh takes. On Sundays, they have a culture swap: introducing each other to a TV series, book, film, album, play or podcast with which they’re obsessed. Hollie Richardson Widely available, episodes twice-weekly from Thursday 19 November Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Strangers gave me £2,409’: the online community helping people in debt
articles.description: People come together online to support one another with small voluntary donations to ease financial worries For some time people struggling with debt have used social media to document what they owe, swap advice and hold themselves accountable as they try to pay it off. Some have built large audiences around their repayment journeys, using views and engagement to generate income through creator payment schemes, livestream gifts and donations from followers towards their debts. Now the idea is being taken a step further: rather than one person building an audience to help clear their own debt, strangers are creating communities to help pay off one another’s. Continue reading...

articles.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
articles.description: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples. Cont

articles.title: DWP glitch threatens my partner’s leave to remain
articles.description: Government department admits it is making a mistake that affects his immigration status but says it can’t put it right The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is knowingly paying me too much local housing allowance because of a system glitch and it could have serious implications for my partner’s immigration status. I am entitled to shared accommodation allowance as I am under 35 and claim universal credit. However, the DWP is paying me the higher one-bedroom rate for couples. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tell us: have you been misdiagnosed with a medical condition?
articles.description: We are looking for people to share their stories of misdiagnosis, how they realised this had happened, and perhaps found another diagnosis Last month the actor Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis . She announced that she had the condition in 2021, and has spoken candidly about her experiences of it, becoming a prominent advocate for people living with MS. “I’m back at square one ... I don’t know what’s going on with me.” Applegate said on her podcast MeSsy, adding: “There’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
articles.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting

articles.title: Naming your feelings can be harder than you think. This simple tool can help
articles.description: About 10% of people have significant trouble identifying their emotions – which makes it harder to know what to do about them Naming emotions is a core skill that most people develop as children, and it might seem like second nature. But research indicates that it’s harder than you think – about 10% of the general population have significant difficulty identifying their own emotions. That’s why a simple tool called the feelings wheel has gained popularity in therapists’ offices and classrooms over recent years. Continue reading...

articles.title: Grammys 2027: Raye, Rosalía and Olivia Rodrigo lead female-heavy nominations
articles.description: The race is led by a number of female artists, also including Phoebe Bridgers and Ella Langley, with Beyoncé receiving her record-breaking 100th nomination Grammys 2027: the nominations in all the major categories Raye is leading this year’s female-heavy Grammys race with 11 nominations. The British singer-songwriter, who has received four nominations in the past, picked up nods in categories including song of the year, songwriter of the year and album of the year. Continue reading...

articles.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
articles.description: Grand Palais, Paris The fair celebrated the bicentenary of photography – but did anyone care? Especially when the most compelling images proposed whole new ways of seeing No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist. This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance. Continue reading...

articles.title: From pyjama parades to blind biscuit taste tests: how we made our ultimate festive gift guide
articles.description: We spent months putting hundreds of presents to the test – here is how we whittled them down • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 If you struggle with the idea of Christmas creep – when the festive season appears to start earlier every year – spare a thought for the team here at Filter HQ. We’ve been in Christmas mode since we packed away last year’s decorations, testing hundreds of presents for our magnum opus: the big 2026 Christmas gift guide . All 369 (we did say it was big) gifts on this year’s list were put through their paces by a crack team of testers covering all ages and tastes. Fashion writer and stylist Sam Deaman – who tested men’s accessories and nightwear – says his partner got fed up with him parading “yet another” pair of pyjamas around their bedroom each night: “It was like Stars in Their Eyes for Christmas gifts,” he says. “‘Tonight, Matthew, I’m going to be … Ebenezer Scrooge!’” Continue reading...

articles.title: The one change that worked: I was burnt out and lonely – until I started ice skating
articles.description: I was stressed and newly diagnosed with ADHD when I decided to choose a new hobby. It awakened my playfulness and immediately improved my quality of life In 2024, I decided to return to England after four and a half years in Lisbon. My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living. During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. I felt overwhelmed and would shut down, which would lead to cycles of anxiety, depression and self-criticism. Continue reading...

articles.title: Share your thoughts on Andy Burnham’s plan for a new EU deal
articles.description: We would like to hear your thoughts on the reopening of the Brexit debate Andy Burnham has announced that he will sign a new deal with the EU , arguing the UK has “lost more than we gained” since Brexit. “This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say at the lord mayor’s banquet in London on Monday, ahead of a summit with European leaders to secure agreements he says could raise GDP by £17bn. Continue reading...

articles.title: The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings
articles.description: If you discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds when consuming fruit and vegetables you are missing out on a lot of value. Here’s what to incorporate into your diet – and what to avoid Do you peel your potatoes, deseed your squash and core your cauliflower? A study by King’s College London , published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition , found that people who routinely discard peels, skins, stalks and seeds when preparing fruit and vegetables are missing out on a valuable source of dietary fibre. Ten out of the 12 types of produce the researchers analysed had higher levels of fibre in the scraps than in the flesh. Eating these often overlooked parts could help address the global dietary fibre deficit and tackle food waste, they say. Here, experts share their advice on how to cook and eat “root to tip”. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘His wife was horrified’: did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?
articles.description: He is the maestro of American melancholy. But in a new biography, the artist is called a ‘sadist’ and a ‘prize hog’ by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.” Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily dia

articles.title: Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so
articles.description: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy unpicked Darwinian sexism to rewrite the story of evolution. Now, she’s turned her attention to the nature of fatherhood ‘Spit here, dear,” Sarah Blaffer Hrdy said to her husband, Dan, handing him a vial when he arrived in New York after the birth of the couple’s first grandchild. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones. It did, although it took a day longer. In her latest book, Father Time: A Natural History of Men and Babies , Hrdy records with justified pride that “this was the first time anyone had demonstrated a bump in oxytocin levels among doting grandparents”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Simply telling the AA about my minor no-fault, no-claim prang doubled my insurance quote
articles.description: A recent £364 renewal quote suddenly increased to an extortionate £796 My car was involved in a minor no-fault accident. The other driver admitted responsibility and said they would pay for repairs without involving insurers. I informed my insurer, the AA, without making a claim. It had recently sent a renewal quote for £364, but after reporting the accident I was sent a revised figure of £796.86. I was told by a call handler that any insurance company would do the same. However, they eventually lowered the quote to £452.31. This seems extortionate for a no-fault, no-claim prang. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sebastián Lelio remembered: ‘He had one hand with the ordinary day-to-day and the other in the heavens’
articles.description: Actor Elaine Cassidy, composer Matthew Herbert and writer Rebecca Lenkiewicz pay tribute to the extraordinary talents of the acclaimed Chilean director, who has died aged 52 Elaine Cassidy, actor, The Wonder Continue reading...

articles.title: Belonging by Sonia Gandhi review – India’s elder stateswoman breaks her silence
articles.description: The Italian who became kingmaker in the world’s largest democracy charts her remarkable journey By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history. No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years. Continue reading...

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the bedbugs that bit me – and worried Jake Gyllenhaal
articles.description: An infestation at my hotel meant my clothes had to be fumigated. When I turned up in shorts to interview the actor, he lent me his jacket, but I suspect he may have regretted it The biting flies were wild in Toronto in September 2012. A colleague and I were there to cover the film festival, but our key reference that year was a zinger from the 2007 cartoon Bee Movie, when it turns out Chris Rock’s mosquito has become a lawyer: “I was already a bloodsucking parasite,” he says, “all I needed was a briefcase!” (Bee Movie is one of the most brilliant and adult children’s movies ever; its central premise compares the honey industry to concentration camps.) Anyway, I spent the first week getting ever more bloodless and lumpy. We even shot a video about them, spraying repellent in front of us like Mace. It didn’t work. Every morning I woke bumpier than before. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. Last month, all that changed. Just not in the way you probably imagine. Continue reading...

articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
articles.description: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge. India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t buy new tech this Black Friday: expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops
articles.description: Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls • How to make your phone last longer Even if you do your best to avoid it, it’s hard to escape the noise of retailers offering implausible-seeming Black Friday discounts on desirable technology. What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be. While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The landslide hit the side of my car. I heard screaming, and realised it was me’ – This is climate breakdown
articles.description: She set off for home in bright sunshine in British Columbia, Canada. Then the rains came – and the mud. This is Chelsey Sharpe’s story Location: Agassiz , Canada Disaster: Southern British Columbia floods, 2021 In 2021, Chelsey Sharpe was working part-time as a yoga instructor when a mudslide swept her car off the highway. Climate change made the heavy rains behind that mudslide and the 2021 floods across southern British Columbia more likely. Continue reading...

articles.title: A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese
articles.description: Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side. Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food. Continue reading...

articles.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
articles.description: The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’ ‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.” On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers .” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
articles.description: Royal Academy, London The modernist collector once ran a gallery in London – but from this confusing exhibition, it’s hard to tell what exactly was once in there Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky , Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy . How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful o

articles.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
articles.description: Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed . Continue reading...

articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed und

articles.title: Help! Why does my apple pie always have a soggy base? | Kitchen aide
articles.description: Direct the heat and minimise the moisture to save your pastry from a saturated bottom, says our panel of pie pros Why does the pastry base of my apple pie always come out soggy? What am I doing wrong? Sophie, by email “The very first thing I would say is that Sophie has got to look at her filling, and how wet it is,” says Calum Franklin, author of The Modern Pie Maker and all-round pie Yoda. “Apples contain quite a lot of water already, so you don’t generally need to add any extra liquid to the filling.” Instead, he’d simply cook the apples with sugar: “Just let them break down.” That said, Sophie could always consider including some sort of barrier, too, says Dee Rettali, co-founder of Fortitude Bakehouse in London: “My mother was an amazing baker, and she always sprinkled a very fine crumble mix [just sugar and flour, no fat] on the bottom of her pie before putting in any fruit. That will then absorb most of the liquid.” Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com Continue reading...

articles.title: After Eight: the story of Satpal Ram - documentary
articles.description: It is 40 years since a racially charged attack at a curry house led to Satpal Ram’s conviction for murder, but today Britain’s post-pub curry culture still has a dark side. Ram spent 24 years in prison before a global campaign for justice, led by bands including Asian Dub Foundation and Primal Scream, secured his release from prison. His case raises crucial questions about the UK’s ongoing struggle for racial equality Continue reading...

articles.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.description: With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south. Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions. Continue reading...

articles.title: The 45 best Secret Santa gifts in the UK for £15 or less – tried and tested for 2026
articles.description: From grippy socks and posh condiments to beautiful stationery and accessories, these affordable Christmas presents are anything but naff • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 Secret Santa is an amazing concept to reduce the amount of gifts you feel obliged to buy, but I find it can result in quite a bit of tat. Resist the urge to buy a joke gift – often instant landfill – and use your budget to get your recipient something useful, or that feels quite treat-y. I’m assuming for this guide that the rules of Secret Santa are that you know who your recipient is – they just don’t know who the gift is from. That is helpful as you can tailor it to their tastes and hobbies. If it’s blind both ways, food is always well received, and socks – while a Christmas cliche – are something everyone wants a new pair of (just get the best you can afford, not, as one of my family used to do, just restock my black school socks). Continue reading...

articles.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
articles.description: Company issues first earnings report after ouster of CEO over allegations of affair with suspected Chinese spy Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster. Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
articles.description: Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country. The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs
articles.description: Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes. Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu. Continue reading...

articles.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
articles.description: The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over. Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. articles.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
articles.description: Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the  $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year. “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis , ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they exp

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
articles.description: This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate. Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work , he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit. articles.title: Sleep paralysis: when you’re awake, but can’t move – or even breathe | Letters
articles.description: Readers recount their terrifying experiences of sleep paralysis in response to an article by Amy Fleming I experienced sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations from childhood and into adulthood, with the episodes only waning in my 30s ( Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis, 11 November ). I never spoke about them to anyone. I experienced hallucinations in the form of severe perspective distortion (oversized bed and rooms) and full hallucinations/dream states, auditory hallucinations (screaming and loud thumping) and, of course, paralysis. I didn’t know at what point I was asleep or if I had woken and could easily slip back into a hypnagogic state. I only became aware of this state as an adult, having been referred to a psychiatrist on an unrelated matter. Continue reading...

Chefs on eight easy things to do now – so you can relax on the big day, 12 November ) with a mixture of disbelief and mounting despair. Apparently, the secret to a stress-free Christmas involves roasting a kilogram of chicken wings and simmering stock for hours, making marmalade from scratch, infusing gin with Sichuan peppercorns and, should we have a spare afternoon, heading into the woods to forage for Douglas fir needles. The city of the Prince Bishops, Durham, would be an ideal choice. We already have a ready-made and renovated “pitman’s parliament” debating chamber and offices in the historic Redhills building of the Durham Miners’ Association. This is only a five-minute walk from the railway station, which has hourly trains to all points south, including nearby Darlington with its “Treasury North” office, so very convenient. articles.title: ‘How can we make it riskier?’: the trans theatre troupe turning Virginia Woolf’s Orlando into a ‘porno-biography’
articles.description: A radical new take on the modernist classic includes a Berlin ketamine binge, a ‘goon cave’ and an all-trans cast. The manifesto? To ‘desecrate’ expectations As Orlando’s on a comedown after a ket-heavy night out in Berlin, surrounded by a group of sharp-tongued trans sex workers, Charli Cowgill and Laurie Ward pause the read-through. The scene is new and “it’s feeling a little safe,” Ward says, drumming the table. “How can we make it riskier?” Cowgill and Ward are piss/CARNATION, a theatre-making duo creating fearless, messy and intellectually rigorous work. Audience spit was collected and thrown in their first production, 52 Monologues for Young Transsexuals , a show that collated trans women’s experiences of men and sex work. Ugly Sisters, the pair’s riotous follow-up, relived a brief encounter between a trans woman and Germaine Greer who wrote a caustic article about it. “As a company,” Ward says, “we tend more towards brutal than twee.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Call my (estate) agent! Why celebrities are always buying each other’s homes

The month before, Brad Pitt bought a mansion from one of the Killers. In 2022, Adele bought Sylvester Stallone’s old house, but only if he let her keep his Rocky statue. Aaron Paul recently sold a house that he bought from The Big Bang Theory’s Jim Parsons, who bought it from Robert Pattinson, after it was previously owned by Noah Wyle, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Tim Curry and the guy who directed Legally Blonde. If this makes it sound to you as if there are only a handful of celebrity-friendly homes on earth, and celebrities spend their lives swapping them around among themselves, then you’re right. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tell us: did you move to the countryside for retirement and come to regret it?

He urged people to think carefully about the challenges of rural life as they get older, including poor access to healthcare, limited public transport and the risk of becoming isolated or dependent on others. We want to hear from the people people who have experienced these challenges. Did you move to the countryside for your retirement and find it more difficult to access the services and support you need? Are you feeling dependent on others to get around and access amenities, leaving you wishing you’d stayed in a town or city? Or have you moved back to a city, finding rural life too isolating as you become older? Continue reading...

Now is your chance When he first charmed audiences in 2001 as phenomenally relatable everyman Tim in a lo-fi BBC mockumentary about office workers, he did so as a hugely loved supporting character. It wasn’t a given that he’d go on to be one of Britain’s most beloved actors, with a role in the highest grossing movie franchise ever, multiple Emmy wins and end up outshining everyone else who shared the screen with him. Yet, in the decades since, that’s just what’s happened: Martin Freeman has starred in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, won one of his two Baftas for being the Dr Watson to Benedict Cumberbatch’s Sherlock Holmes and somehow become a cornerstone of Christmas, with roles in Richard Curtis’s Love Actually and Nativity. articles.description: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game?
