It could be a tipping point in the industry The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
articles.description: He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original ‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.” Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles rel

articles.title: Nicola Coughlan on her favourite noodles, getting rejected from drama school and I Am Helen
articles.description: What does Lady Whistledown eat when nobody's watching?  This week on Comfort Eating, Siobhán McSweeney is joined by the brilliant Nicola Coughlan, star of Derry Girls and Bridgerton, for a seriously fun catch-up involving comfort food, childhood nostalgia and some VERY questionable food combinations. Nicola brings her ultimate comfort food to the table: think fusion - or perhaps it’s confusion. There's also Diet Coke mixed with pickle juice (yes, really), stories about growing up in Galway, and her Supermac's Gold Card. Plus, Nicola reflects on her journey into acting, drama school rejection, the early struggles of making it in London and how life changed after Derry Girls and Bridgerton. Continue reading...

articles.title: Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet | Mark Mon-Williams
articles.description: As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms. The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxie

articles.title: Macron banned smartphones in schools. A month later, France was ablaze. Could they be connected? | Joseph de Weck
articles.description: French teachers argue that a digital detox woke students up to the decrepit state of their schools – and drove them out into the streets Remember the 1999 blockbuster The Matrix ? It may be more than a quarter of a century old, but it has become a byword and a meme for a frighteningly plausible kind of 21st-century tech dystopia. A quick recap: the computer hacker Neo discovers that machines rule over humanity. They keep people trapped in pods, their minds immersed in a virtual reality designed to keep them docile (the “Matrix” of the title). Once he becomes aware of the world he actually inhabits, Neo decides to take up arms. Continue reading...

articles.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
articles.description: After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI . But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes. Continue reading...

articles.title: Child doping isn’t just cheating – it’s a global epidemic of abuse and exploitation | Sean Ingle
articles.description: Surveys estimate 10 million minors globally use banned performance-enhancing drugs but suppliers are rarely brought to justice Of all the many stories in Doping Top Secret: Children, a powerful new documentary from the German investigative team that helped expose massive Russian cheating in sport over a decade ago, one keeps replaying in my mind. It involves an East German champion, who breaks his silence half a century on from his Olympic triumph to reveal how being pumped full of anabolic steroids at a young age accelerated his sexual development and, he believes, dramatically altered his behaviour and those of his teammates. “The system abused me as a young person for the good of the state,” says Hans-Georg Aschenbach, who won ski-jump gold in Innsbruck in 1976. Although nothing can prepare you for what he says about how the drugs affected his libido, and particularly what he would sometimes do before he jumped off a large ramp. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe | Rafael Behr
articles.description: In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” . Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’? |
articles.description: Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering. Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home. Continue reading...

articles.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description: The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while , and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down. Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire . I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company , Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m). Continue reading...

articles.title: Duckett’s bold 133 steers England to ODI series win as sandpapergate latest rocks Australia
articles.description: As per Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg, upon announcing the creation of a forum for players to share memories of sandpaper in South Africa eight years ago, two diametrically opposed versions of events can both be true. By that logic, anyone remembering this deciding one-day international in Hobart as a win for Australia in years to come will not technically be wrong. It will simply be “their truth”, to use an overused phrase in this saga. Continue reading...

articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz v Daniil Medvedev: ATP Finals tennis group stage – live
articles.description: ATP Finals updates, with play in Turin from 2pm GMT Sign up and get The Recap newsletter | Email Daniel I’ve just seen Henman’s post-Tiafoe interview with Alcaraz; “I felt fantastic out there,” he said. Oof madone, what it must be like to experience that, and to feel comfortable saying it because it’s self-evidently true. I’m going to start conceiving of liveblogging in that way; “Thanks Tim, I’m feeling really mediocre in here.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi
articles.description: Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career “I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds. Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons. Continue reading...

articles.title: Fifa’s World Cup TV rights documents indicate hydration breaks will stay in 2030
articles.description: Controversial breaks were financial boon for broadcasters Fifa flags possible benefits but says no decision made Fifa’s tender documents for TV rights for the 2030 World Cup includes a provision for broadcasters to sell adverts during hydration breaks in a strong indication the controversial stoppages will be retained. A three-minute break midway through each half was introduced for the first time at all 104 matches at last summer’s World Cup in the interests of player welfare, a radical move that also provided a commercial boon for broadcasters, particularly the rights holders in the United States, Fox Sports and Telemundo. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ireland’s Prendergast free to face South Africa after avoiding hip-drop tackle ban
articles.description: Rassie Erasmus had predicted player would be cleared South Africa Rugby condemns online abuse of officials Ireland’s fly-half Sam Prendergast is available to face South Africa in the Nations Championship on Saturday after his citing for an alleged hip-drop tackle against Fiji was dismissed. Prendergast was cited for the challenge on Fiji’s captain Peceli Yato under a new offence added to Law 9.13 at the start of November. However, following a hearing on Tuesday, an independent disciplinary committee decided no further action would be taken against the 23-year-old, who could have been hit with a suspension. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jack Grealish recalls a golden age of mavericks – but football has moved on
articles.description: Everton forward has magical talent and popularity to burn, but has come up against hard reality of the modern game Thomas Tuchel has never called up the player he once claimed to love “everything about”. The reason for Jack Grealish’s omission from Tuchel’s first England squad in March 2025 was given as “he simply has no rhythm”. Catch a falling star? Grealish was suspended by Everton for three matches following “a breach of club discipline”. Suggestions his loan from Manchester City might be cancelled were calmed by David Moyes. Last week, Grealish played in a behind-closed doors friendly against Derby before issuing an Instagram statement: “I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.” Amid tabloid tales of karaoke nights and extended socialising, how close is the former boy wonder, now 31, to blowing it? Continue reading...

articles.title: Overlap, underlap or sit back? How Premier League teams use their full-backs
articles.description: The role of full-back has changed massively in recent years. We analyse how all 20 sides are approaching the position By Opta Analyst Overlapping. Underlapping. Inverted. Traditional. The role of full-back has evolved dramatically. Once a defensive-first position that provided some auxiliary attacking support, the role has developed into something far more multifaceted. Just ask right-back Ben White, who – with Riccardo Calafiori on the left – has been an important figure in Arsenal’s superb start to the campaign. Talking a few years ago, he said: “Playing full-back the way [Mikel Arteta] wants is completely different to any other manager. To play full-back for him, you’ve got to be a centre-midfielder, a centre-back, a winger and a No 10.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge
articles.description: Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more Mail us with all of your questions and answers “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?” The gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. Wales and Northern Ireland both moved up 109 places: Wales from 117th to eighth under Gary Speed and then Chris Coleman, Northern Ireland from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017. 183 places Montenegro (16th/199th) 165 Kuwait (24/189) 160 Bosnia and Herzegovina (13/173) 155 Cape Verde (27/182) 153 Central African Republic (49/202) 151 Libya (36/187) 146 Equatorial Guinea (49/195) 144 Moldova (37/181) 141 El Salvador (49/190) 136 Cuba (46/182), Slovakia (14/150) Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Ten is the minimum’: 14-year-old surfing champion Leihani Zoric aims for record world title haul
articles.description: Zoric puts target on veteran teammate Gilmore’s back: ‘I want to be like her’ Peru win makes her first Indigenous Australian world champion in open category With the surfing world her oyster, Leihani Zoric has set her sights stratospherically high after the 14-year-old stunned a star-studded field to be crowned the youngest ever ISA Open World Surfing Champion and claim a second world title this year. Zoric, who was still 13 when she won the ISA under-18 world title in September, added a gold medal to her burgeoning individual palmarès with victory in Peru over the weekend, when she emerged triumphant ahead of established stars of the surfing world such as Stephanie Gilmore, Tyler Wright, Carissa Moore and Johanne Defay. Continue reading...

articles.title: All EU members should back €45bn loan for Ukraine, says von der Leyen – Europe live
articles.description: Commission president says even countries that do not wish to support Ukraine militarily can still provide funding for civilian part of loan Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii ⁠Sybiha urged China and the United ⁠States ​to apply pressure on Russia to end its ⁠war in Ukraine. Chinese president Xi Jinping , US ⁠president Donald Trump and Russian ​president ‌ Vladimir Putin ‌ are due to hold a ‌trilateral meeting on Thursday in China’s southern city of Shenzhen. Continue reading...

articles.title: Russian attacks have left Kyiv with devastating power outages – and its mayor in a perilous position
articles.description: As Ukraine’s capital suffers through an energy crisis, many blame Vitali Klitschko for failing to prepare for winter Maksym Bakhmatov, the outspoken head of one of Kyiv’s largest city districts, did not mince his words when it came to who was responsible for the devastating power outages plaguing his area’s 600,000 residents. “First, because of Putin,” he said from his office in Desnianskyi, a working-class area on Kyiv’s left bank. “Second, because of lack of normal management from the mayor, [Vitali Klitschko]. That’s it.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The voice of a nation: the Czech children’s TV show that became a symbol of media freedom
articles.description: Večerníček has wished children goodnight for 60 years, and now his distinctive newspaper hat symbolises the fight for the future of public broadcasting Photos of the mass rallies in support of Czech public broadcasters in recent weeks have featured one detail that has baffled outsiders: demonstrators wearing little hats made out of folded newspapers. But to Czechs they are instantly recognisable. The hat belongs to Večerníček, a little cartoon boy who appears on Czech Television every evening at 6.45pm. Continue reading...

articles.title: Nasa’s Voyager 1 just reached a massive milestone in space - video
articles.description: Nasa sent the Voyager 1 and 2 probes into space almost 50 years ago to explore the outer reaches of our solar system. Now Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object from Earth, is about to reach a distance of one light-day away from our planet. To find out more about its astonishing journey, Madeleine Finlay hears from Jim Bell, a planetary scientist and professor at Arizona State University’s school of Earth and space exploration. He explains the seismic impact the mission has had on our understanding of the solar system, and where Voyager 1 could be heading now it has left the heliosphere Continue reading...

articles.title: Scores of children who lived at religious sect’s compound are subject of care proceedings
articles.description: Cases in UK family court relating to Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light follow police raid in April Scores of children linked to a religious sect raided by police over allegations of serious sexual offences and modern slavery are now the subject of care proceedings, court documents have revealed. Family courts were dealing with more than 40 cases in relation to “a very significant number of children” who were living at the compound run by the Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light (AROPL) when it was raided by police in April. Continue reading...

articles.title: Yvette Cooper announces new health support for most vulnerable people in England
articles.description: Health secretary says 500,000 will benefit initially from ‘downpayment’ on PM’s national care service pledge UK politics live – latest updates Half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will get proactive help with their health needs from new teams that will act as a “downpayment” on the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced. Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive help from new joint teams of NHS and social care staff. Initially about 500,000 people by next April will benefit from new joined-up support teams providing personalised care. Continue reading...

articles.title: £10m ‘once-in-a-generation’ study to explore effects of children’s social media ban
articles.description: Research to look at whether ban can make meaningful change in mental health and wellbeing for under-16s Countries around the world are considering social media bans for children, but whether this would work in practice has been hotly debated. Now researchers are seeking answers through a major scientific study led by Wellcome, which will be the first of its kind. Ten research projects will explore topics ranging from children’s mental health to their sleep and physical activity, comparing factors before and after the social media ban for children under 16 is introduced in the UK in spring 2027. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘My family would kill me if they saw it’: the ‘harmless’ images that can be deadly for women in Pakistan
articles.description: Tech companies urged to adapt moderation of photos online that can trigger violence against women in some countries It was just a photo of a smiling girl in jeans and a vest top, the kind of outfit any young woman might wear in any country. But for Maniza*, a teenager from a conservative town in Pakistan who never leaves the house without her hijab, the selfie she took at home put her at very real risk of an “honour” killing. “My family are really strict and I always wore a hijab. My father didn’t want me to stay in school but my mum pushed him. He said if I got into trouble, he would kill me. It wasn’t just words, he meant it,” she says. Continue reading...

articles.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
articles.description: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs. Continue reading...

articles.title: This Muslim civil rights group defended pro-Palestine protesters. Then Florida labeled it a terrorist organization
articles.description: Cair-Florida is suing state officials after designation meant it had to shut its doors to victims of harassment and discrimination Omar Soboh, a student at the University of Florida, was organizing a campus panel about Islamophobia when he found out one of the groups being represented had suddenly been blacklisted by the state. Under a new process, Florida had designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a domestic terrorist organization. The university’s Arab Students’ Association decided to cancel the event, and Soboh, who is Palestinian American, was disheartened. “Our existence itself is political,” he said. Continue reading...

articles.title: Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.description: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya. The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. Continue reading...

articles.title: SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site unless ministers intervene
articles.description: Energy firm says existing market arrangements do not sustain facility’s continued operation The energy company SSE has warned it will close its Atwick natural gas storage facility in northern England next summer, if the government does not intervene to offer support amid weak market conditions. The site, located near Hornsea on the East Yorkshire coast, consists of eight caverns with the capacity to store about 309m cubic metres of gas, estimated at about 1.5 days’ worth of Great Britain’s gas usage. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel
articles.description: The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film. NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have already seen it in cinemas and its Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have picked up a roster of prestigious awards. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet, amid a severe backlash. Continue reading...

articles.title: Valerie Solanas’s obscenely funny Scum Manifesto is an unignorable burst of female outrage | Emily Woof
articles.description: Before an assassination attempt on Andy Warhol in 1968, Solanas used her fierce writing to confront male supremacy. What can her work teach us about expressing raw anger? It is exhausting to always express anger constructively and reasonably – especially when what you are angry about is violence, exploitation and the inexcusable appetite of disgusting, powerful, greedy men to gain yet more power. Could you please be more balanced in how you express yourself? Could you make your objection to the destruction of the world – through violating not only women but also the planet – well, more constructive? Could you be a little less unpleasant in your anger? Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The aesthetics in my family were so high, I felt ugly’: Charlotte Gainsbourg on extremism, abortion and her mother, Jane Birkin
articles.description: In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier While she was making the film Women on Trial , about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France. The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.” Continue reading...

articles.title: From Dumb Starbucks to dada documentary: everything you need to know about Nathan Fielder
articles.description: With the UK release of You Can See Everything looming, now’s an ideal time to get up to speed on the bizarre, puckish and very meta comedic oeuvre of its star “There are three sides to every story: your side, my side, and the truth. And no one is lying. Memories shared serve each differently.” Those words were spoken by film producer Robert Evans – but nobody has ever interrogated the idea more skilfully than comedian Nathan Fielder. The three-hour documentary You Can See Everything – co-directed by and starring Fielder – opens in the UK on Friday, having already become an unlikely cultural phenomenon and box office sensation in the US. The film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her beginning a prison sentence for defrauding investors; what emerges is a profound meditation on the nature of truth and the fundamental unknowability of other human beings. To view the film as being simply about the Theranos scandal is akin to considering Casablanca merely a movie about a nightclub. And, as one might expect given Fielder’s background, it’s hilarious. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘We want our story to be told’: inside a shocking 36-year fight for justice in Baltimore
articles.description: A staggering case of injustice is explored in the galling HBO documentary When a Witness Recants. The three subjects and producer Ta-Nehisi Coates explain how it unfolded For most of his life, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates would occasionally think of a chilling episode from his childhood in West Baltimore: almost exactly 43 years ago, on 18 November 1983, a 14-year-old boy named DeWitt Duckett was shot and killed in a hallway of Harlem Park junior high school in the middle of the afternoon, by an older teenager who stole his blue satin Georgetown jacket. Coates was only eight years old at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. The sensational event – the first time a kid was killed inside a Baltimore public school, according to wall-to-wall local press – was a rupture in his child’s view of the world. “It was first time I had the sense that, oh, actually, I exist in a very dangerous world,” he told the Guardian. “And then you cut to the TV and it’s clear the rest of America is not existing in that dangerous world. The dangerous world is only for you and people who look like you.” Coates always assumed that the three teena

articles.title: Josephine review – Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan ballast knotty drama about a child witness to a rape
articles.description: Mason Reeves steals the show as an eight year old who stumbles across a sex assault but, despite strong performances, parts of the film feel contrived Beth de Araújo’s new movie takes a very big swing, and it has won prizes and acclaim since its premiere at Sundance. I was unsure about some of the film’s high-concept ideas but the lead performance from its eight-year-old newcomer Mason Reeves is outstanding. Those concerned about spoilers had better look away. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan play Damien and Claire, a smart professional couple in San Francisco with a bright young daughter called Josephine, marvellously played by Reeves. Damien takes Josephine to Golden Gate Park one morning to play football (they turn out to enjoy watching the English Premier League on TV). She mischievously runs on ahead of her dad to a secluded spot in the park where Damien can’t immediately find her and it is there that Josephine witnesses a rape – not less horrifying for being filmed in long shot. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
articles.description: Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “ gjak ” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

articles.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
articles.description: Scientific discoveries are effortlessly explained in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. Continue reading...

articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You

articles.title: Cosimo I de’Medici review – up close and personal with a Renaissance godfather
articles.description: Wallace Collection, London A sword, a wine cooler, a dazzling fresco … only a museum with such a copious store of treasures could put on a display this rich without having to borrow Mounting a “store-cupboard” exhibition – choosing items from existing collections to make a new, contained display – can be a cheap and easy way for a museum to make something out of its existing resources, without the faff of securing loans or collaborating across the industry. In the case of the Wallace Collection, however, the store cupboard is so embarrassingly rich and diverse that strong displays such as this on Cosimo I de’Medici can be drawn from only a handful of its objects. The 19th-century collection of Sir Richard Wallace holds a notable number of medieval objects, but their display can seem – at least to contemporary eyes – like a cacophony of applied arts, armour and paintings, not to mention a ton of gilt. This Medici display is part of a new enterprise drawing out histories from the noise for singular focus, sensibly repurposing what was once the cloakroom (a previously wasted bit of prime real estate) as a new dedicated space. Continue reading...

articles.title: A moment that changed me: the tomato pasta that became an obsession – and helped me lead a better life
articles.description: At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. I spent four days with his lovely family, in the rolling verdant hills, with fireflies and fallow deer keeping us company, drinking vernaccia and talking of books and art and poetry. But none of that matters, not even a bit. Al

articles.title: Prawn masala and spiced roast cauliflower: Romy Gill’s Indian recipes for chilly nights
articles.description: Spiced prawns cooked in coconut milk and a whole roast cauliflower with almonds and coriander – these dishes take me back to the food of my childhood These two dishes are just the kind of food I want to eat on a chilly evening. The cauliflower is deeply spiced, nutty and comforting, with coconut, almonds, ginger and chilli bringing warmth and texture, while the prawn masala is quicker and lighter, but still full of flavour, with the spices and the sweet prawns coming together beautifully. Both dishes reflect the way I love to cook: generous, vibrant with layers of spice, but never so much that you lose the character of the main ingredient. Continue reading...

articles.title: Life insurance: what is it and do you need it?
articles.description: It could protect you and your family in the event of death or accident – and in some cases it costs no more than a TV streaming service No one wants to spend time imagining the worst thing that could happen, and perhaps that is why about 60% of UK adults have no life insurance, or why more people have pet insurance than have income protection for if they become too sick to work. However, there are certain milestones in life, such as having children or taking on a mortgage, that focus the mind on what might happen if things do go wrong. How would your family manage if you or your partner died? How would you cover the mortgage if you had an accident and couldn’t work? Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: Thrilling views of Iceland’s humpbacks, (perhaps) lured in by Céline Dion | Claire Stares
articles.description: Eyjafjörður: Our boat was surrounded by around 15 of them, exploding their exhalations out of the water – and numbers are increasing here For the first half-hour, Eyjafjörður, Iceland’s longest fjord, offered few signs of marine life – just three cormorants and a raft of common eiders. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A  humpback whale . As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. But, as if on cue, two explosive exhalations erupted alongside the boat, prompting whoops of delight. Continue reading...

articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: Three cheers for Melania Trump-led ceasefire in Ukraine
articles.description: The humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine, mediated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV and jointly implemented by Ukraine and Russia, is unprecedented since the start of this war in 2022. Its success and people-centered spirit also stand in conspicuous contrast to the repeated attempts by the Trump administration to end the war, which have all ended in frustrated failure. There has been pragmatic, if intermittent, engagement between Russia and Ukraine virtually since the 2022 Russian invasion, around issues like the exchange of prisoners of war and the bodies of the fallen, or the Black Sea Grain Initiative . But until October 27, 2026, no humanitarian ceasefire along the frontline had ever been successfully implemented; it had never even been attempted. The story of how Oleshky became a step on the path towards peace has twists and turns. The town on the left bank of the Dnieper River was occupied on the first day of the 2022 Russian invasion. Should we stay the course or escalate? This debate raged through the historic MAGA coalition that brought Donald Trump and JD Vance to the White House. My position on it was clear: the war was the catalyst for my resignation from the Trump administration — and likely for many others who left without making their disagreement public. This debate burned hot and loudly in right wing circles online, on podcasts and occasionally even on right-wing mainstream platforms like Fox News. Then suddenly, on Tuesday night, after months of deafening argument, all of that debate was suddenly silenced, like a father coming home from work telling bickering siblings to knock off the racket. The American people loudly rejected the war by voting against President Trump’s Republican party and handing the Democrats a historic landslide, granting them solid control of the House and Senate. articles.title: When the 'Watergate Babies' rode their own wave of anger
articles.description: If foreign-policy restrainers of both parties are looking for a model the new Congress can follow once it takes office in January, they could do worse than to refer back to the 1974 midterm election that brought to Washington a tidal wave of young Democrats who quickly passed legislation placing unprecedented constraints on the power of the “Imperial Presidency,” which had reached its zenith under former President Richard Nixon. In many respects, the parallels between the 1974 midterms and the results of Tuesday’s election are eerie. Though Nixon, whose own imperial pretensions were more sartorial than architectural , had resigned from office three months before the vote, his abuses of executive powers loomed large over the election. Those abuses were, after all, hard to ignore: from Watergate and the impoundment of Congressional appropriations at home, to the secret bombing of Cambodia and Laos and the covert CIA campaign to overthrow the democratically-elected government of Chile abroad. articles.description: The Post-1945 World Order Is Breaking Apart... Authored by Nick Giambruno via International Man , Here is my view of the Big Picture as the US-led world order, which has existed since 1945, enters terminal decline . We're likely to see the major global powers - Russia, China, and the US - consolidate power within their respective spheres of influence while competing for strategic advantage outside them. It's important to recognize that geopolitical forecasts deal in probabilities, not certainties. Nothing guarantees that Russia will control Eastern Europe and parts of Central Asia, that China will dominate East Asia, or that the US will turn the Western Hemisphere into its fortress. But that's the way to bet. In other words, will China and Russia stake everything on propping up their Latin American allies? I think Venezuela proves they won't , and that's the wise choice. articles.description: The "Dementia Belt" Where Alzheimer's Epidemic Is Exploding - And Aging Isn't The Only Culprit The dementia epidemic sweeping across parts of the United States may be driven by far more than aging , with geography, cardiovascular health and economic conditions emerging as potentially important factors, according to the Daily Mail . An analysis of Medicare records has exposed a striking geographical divide in dementia diagnoses, with some states reporting nearly twice the rates of others among residents over 65 . The findings raise uncomfortable questions about the long-term consequences of America's chronic disease epidemic. More than seven million Americans currently live with Alzheimer's disease, a figure projected to nearly double over the next 25 years. However, the geographical breakdown reveals something particularly troubling. Seven of the 11 states traditionally associated with America's notorious "stroke belt" also rank among the 15 states with the highest recorded dementia rates. articles.description: Stephen Nolan’s groundbreaking program ‘Peelers’ has certainly shone a light on the reality of policing for the PSNI on the ground. For some, the BBC programme films people at their most vulnerable, others say it’s ‘copaganda’, but other viewers think it is a valuable insight into the circumstances police officers find themselves in. articles.title: ‘All I could smell was fertiliser’: the best (and worst) supermarket instant coffee, tasted and rated
articles.description: Our coffee snob spills the beans on which granules hint at chocolate and caramel, and which leave a bitter note • Everything you need to make great coffee I’m a coffee snob with my own grinder, but I found the haptic thwack, whack and crack of opening the lid and film on a jar of instant coffee strangely invigorating, and rather nostalgic. When I took a deep sniff, however, disaster: all I could smell was fertiliser! Instant coffee is brewed at scorching temperatures, then either freeze-dried in a vacuum or spray-dried using hot air. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. This gives it an earthier, muskier and more bitter flavour profile, though, thankfully, with a little alchemy and hot water, those more familiar coffee aromas and flavours returned, with notes of chicory, bitter chocolate and burnt sugar. Almost all of these products have a similar industrial imprint, uniform granules and a one-dimensional flavour profile, so they’re ultimately more a simulation of the real thing. That said, some did surprise me. At best, they taste like a cup of office filter coffee, made in a commercial d

articles.title: ‘You have to cope’: why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
articles.description: The world has become accustomed to concerns about the male loneliness epidemic. But research suggests women are just as lonely Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads No one would think of Sasha* as lonely, least of all Sasha herself. The 38-year-old from Sydney has close and longstanding friendships, proactively keeps in touch and makes plans, and is engaged with her local community. “All those things that you read about, about why men might be lonely – they don’t maintain one-on-one friendships, or they’re not good at reaching out, or their conversations aren’t deep and meaningful – none of those issues apply to me,” she says. “I’m a very socially connected person.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Who’s duping whom? Cut-price versions of luxury items are Christmas hit
articles.description: From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cheaper dupes of high-end goods have gone mainstream. But is it fair? For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries. But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25. Continue reading...

articles.title: Our five-year-old has hearing loss and may one day be blind. Here is where I find hope
articles.description: Ali Stevens’ daughter was a baby when they discovered she has a syndrome which causes deafblindness. There’s no roadmap for change – but what gets her through is the same as for any parent Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads My daughter Poppy is five. She’s energetic and curious, loves dresses, books and creating new things and spends a lot of time playing with her big sister, Evie. When Poppy was born, my husband, Ben, and I were focused on the usual joys of welcoming a new baby. A routine hearing screening showed something wasn’t quite right, although initially we were told it was probably fluid in her ears. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart
articles.description: Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece , with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February. “We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
articles.description: Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out. It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.
